prompt.context: Our client, Dopamine, is the fourth largest manufacturer of drugs internationally. Two years ago, Dopamine invented a drug — tentatively branded Soma — to treat acute depression. Unlike most antidepressants, the drug is preventative rather than responsive. Whereas most antidepressants attempt to treat diagnosed cases of depression, Soma is designed for consumption before symptoms emerge. It is aimed at individuals who are deemed 'high risk' for acute depression due to family history, an acute trauma, or a variety of other factors. The drug is available by prescription only and it has no known side effects. Soma received regulatory approval by the FDA, and Dopamine is considering how to price the drug in the United States.
prompt.question: You have been asked to size the market and recommend a price for Soma.

clarifying_info.q: Is the drug currently covered by insurance?
clarifying_info.a: The drug has not yet been covered by insurance.

clarifying_info.q: What are the medical costs associated with acute depression?
clarifying_info.a: Medical bills for acute depression average $10,000 annually per case (includes drugs, therapy, and hospitalization).

clarifying_info.q: What were the development costs for the drug?

clarifying_info.a: The drug is a single tablet taken on a daily basis.

framework: Market: size the US market for acute depression, identify competitor/substitute drugs, estimate potential market share for Soma
Product: assess Soma's strengths (preventative, no side effects, FDA-approved, unique mechanism) and weaknesses (novel concept, unproven adoption, no insurance coverage yet)

Pricing model: evaluate price-based pricing (value to insurer vs. current treatment cost) and cost-based pricing (variable cost + margin); determine whether insurers will cover the drug as a key gating factor

questions.prompt: What factors are most critical to the price of Soma?
questions.guidance: Strong answers should mention: uniqueness / lack of substitutes; degree of public and physician acceptance of a preventative mental-health drug; whether insurers will cover Soma (key issue — without coverage the drug will not gain traction); regulatory environment; competing treatments; development cost recovery. Guide toward insurance coverage if not raised.

questions.prompt: How would an insurance company decide whether to cover Soma?
questions.guidance: The insurer's decision is fundamentally a cost comparison: is the total cost under the new drug model lower than the cost under the current treatment-only model? The insurer compares (a) paying for Soma for all high-risk individuals plus treating the failures vs. (b) paying $10,000 per diagnosed acute depression case.

questions.prompt: A price of $50 per package (10 pills) has been proposed. Would an insurer cover the drug at this price if it bore the full cost? Use: 300M US population; 1 in 200 Americans suffer acute depression; 1 in 100 are at-risk, of whom 1 in 5 are high-risk (assume all high-risk develop depression without treatment); Soma is 70% effective; 30% who take Soma and still develop depression cost $10,000 each in addition to Soma costs; all depression cases receive treatment.
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute current insurer costs and new-drug insurer costs, then compare. Current cost < new cost means insurer will not cover; current cost > new cost means insurer will cover.

math.setup: Compare current annual insurer cost vs. annual cost under new Soma treatment model.
steps: Soma cost for high-risk: 600,000 × ($50/10 pills) × 365 days = $1.095B ≈ $1B
Current cost ($15B) > new-drug cost (~$12B), so insurers would likely cover the drug.
math.answer: Current insurer cost ≈ $15B; new-drug model cost ≈ $12B. Insurer saves ~$3B, so coverage is justified at $50/package.

questions.prompt: What would you charge for the drug? Could Dopamine get more than $50?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer. One approach: raise price until new-drug total cost equals current costs ($15B). Another consideration: adoption risk means pricing lower may be prudent early. Key is logical reasoning — e.g., the savings gap of ~$3B implies room to raise prices before insurers balk. Demonstrates intuition and creativity.

questions.prompt: What single factor would allow Dopamine to raise prices?
questions.guidance: Improved screening. Currently only 1 in 100 are identified as at-risk, of whom 1 in 5 are high-risk (1/500 of total population), while 1 in 200 actually develop depression. Better identification of at-risk individuals would increase the pool of Soma users and reduce unidentified cases treated conventionally, shifting cost savings to the insurer and supporting a higher price.

questions.prompt: A client liaison argues that the $500M development cost must be covered by future revenues or Dopamine should not proceed with large-scale production. Is this correct?
questions.guidance: No. The $500M is a sunk cost — it has already been spent and is irrelevant to the go-forward production decision. What matters is whether revenues from sales cover variable costs of production. The correct framework is marginal revenue vs. marginal cost.

questions.prompt: Variable cost of production is $10 per package of 10 pills; fixed costs are zero. What is the margin? What is the markup?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish margin (profit as % of price) from markup (profit as % of cost).

questions.prompt: Indulging the client: given sunk development costs of $500M and assuming a negligible discount rate, what is the breakeven period?
questions.guidance: Use annual profit from Soma sales to the high-risk population, then divide $500M by annual profit.

math.setup: Annual profit = units sold × profit per unit. High-risk population = 600,000; price = $50/package; cost = $10/package; 1 package = 10 pills; 1 pill/day.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors are most critical to the price of Soma?

categories.name: Market & Competitive Factors
ideas: Lack of direct substitutes (first preventative antidepressant)
Market share achievable given novel preventative positioning

categories.name: Adoption & Acceptance
ideas: Public willingness to take a daily pill before symptoms appear
Physician comfort prescribing a preventative psychiatric drug
Stigma around mental health prevention drugs

categories.name: Insurance & Payor Dynamics
ideas: Whether insurers cover the drug (key gating factor)
Insurer cost-benefit analysis vs. current treatment

categories.name: Pricing & Cost Factors
ideas: Sunk R&D cost ($500M) — not relevant to pricing but shapes stakeholder expectations
Value-based pricing ceiling set by insurer savings

recommendation: Dopamine should price Soma at or near $50 per package to maximize insurer coverage and adoption; the drug saves insurers approximately $3B annually at this price, making coverage likely
At $50, the drug achieves an 80% gross margin and recoups $500M in development costs within roughly 7–8 months
risks: Insurer refusal to cover at prices much above $50 would severely limit adoption
Only 600,000 high-risk individuals are currently identified; limited screening infrastructure constrains market size
30% of treated patients still develop depression, creating residual treatment liability
Physician and patient acceptance of a preventative psychiatric drug is uncertain
next_steps: Negotiate insurance coverage agreements citing the $3B annual cost savings to insurers
Invest in improved diagnostic screening to expand the identifiable at-risk population and support future price increases
Conduct physician education campaigns to accelerate prescription adoption
Monitor effectiveness data to build the evidence base for label expansion or price renegotiation
